column3: The earliest historical references to mu in Korea, in the Yisanggugjip and the Samguk sagi, date to the 12th century; they describe spirit mediumship, exorcism, divination and ancestor veneration.
Under the Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1897) Confucian elites suppress the mudang, who belong to one of eight outcast groups expelled from the capital.
The Jeju governor Yi Hyŏngsang purges the island's simbang and destroys 129 shrines (1702).
Modernisers, many of them Christian, call Musok misin, superstition; in 1896 police arrest mudang, destroy shrines and burn paraphernalia.
Under Japanese occupation Musok is suppressed, while scholars begin to present it as Korea's ancient religion.
The Korean War and the division of Korea move many mudang about the peninsula; in North Korea mudang are labelled part of the hostile class.
New Community Movement policing of mudang in South Korea surges, while folklore studies lead more South Koreans to accept Musok as Korea's ancient religion.
Mudang from South Korea begin pilgrimages to Mount Paektu in China, and mudang advertise on the Internet.
South Korea recognises ten regional gut styles as intangible cultural heritage, and the Yŏngdŭng gut on Jeju is added to UNESCO's list.
